items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Industrial Wastewater Treatment: Bibliometric Trends, Application Areas, and Critical Gaps (2016–2025)
items.abstract: The growing complexity and variability of industrial wastewater (IWW) require treatment strategies that can support reliable prediction, monitoring, optimization, and operational decision-making. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have increasingly been applied to these functions; however, the literature remains fragmented across pollutants, treatment processes, and modeling approaches. This study presents a critical bibliometric review of 151 Scopus-indexed publications on AI/ML applications in IWW treatment published between 2016 and 2025. Publication output increased substantially, reaching 35 publications in 2024 and 67 in 2025, compared with 1–4 publications annually during 2016–2019. China was the leading contributor with 54 publications, followed by India with 26, while Saudi Arabia and the United States each contributed 15. The main research directions included prediction and soft sensing, process optimization and control, monitoring and digitalization, adsorption and material-based treatment, membrane processes, and advanced oxidation and degradation. Artificial neural networks, support vector machines, random forests, and hybrid models were among the most frequently applied techniques. Study-level assessment of 38 technically assessable original AI/ML applications showed that 34 studies (89.5%) relied on offline or retrospective model evaluation, whereas only four (10.5%) demonstrated online or real-time AI/ML evaluation or operation. Conventional internal validation predominated among studies for which validation design could be established, while independent temporal, cross-domain, cross-scale, or field-based validation remained comparatively uncommon. Laboratory- and bench-scale applications were common, although several studies used full-scale industrial data. Major barriers to practical deployment include limited transferability across wastewater matrices, insufficient field-scale validation, inconsistent sensor and data quality, limited interpretability, and weak integration with treatment-plant control systems. Chemical oxygen demand soft sensing, pH and chemical-dosing support, and real-time monitoring and anomaly detection represent promising pathways for near-term implementation, while closed-loop control requires stronger validation of reliability, safety, and long-term performance. Overall, the field is transitioning from isolated, model-centered research toward system-level deployment, where transferability, validation, interpretability, and control integration are as important.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Nursing Values: Students’ Perceptions of Trust, Empathy, and Future Roles
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly embedded in healthcare systems, creating new opportunities to enhance efficiency, optimize workflows, and strengthen patient monitoring. At the same time, its integration raises important questions about ethics, trust, and the preservation of humanistic values in nursing practice.Aim: To investigate nursing students’ awareness, attitudes, trust, and visions regarding the integration of AI in healthcare and nursing practice.Methods: A descriptive cross‑sectional design was applied, involving 140 nursing students. Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire that explored awareness, attitudes, trust, and expectations regarding AI in healthcare. The analysis combined descriptive statistics with inferential techniques, including correlation and regression, to identify relationships among the variables.Results: Seventy‑two percent of participants had heard of AI in medicine, but knowledge levels were moderate (M = 3.3). While 43% believed AI could support nurses and 66% saw potential for improved patient care, 60% expressed discomfort with AI‑led care. Empathy and human contact were rated as highly important (M = 3.6 and M = 3.7 respectively), and 83% rejected full replacement of nurses. Trust was limited, with only 32% believing AI reduces medical errors. A majority (57%) envisioned a human‑centered future, with AI serving as a supportive tool rather than a substitute.Conclusion: Nursing students recognize the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) but remain cautious, emphasizing humanistic values and expressing skepticism about safety and trust. They envision a human‑centered future where AI supports nursing practice without replacing its essential human role, highlighting the need for balanced integration through education, policy, and further research.

items.title: Artificial intelligence at the surgeon–pathologist interface: revolutionizing diagnosis, prognostication, and precision surgery
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence applications in surgical pathology encompass tumour detection, histological classification, grading, biomarker assessment, lymph node evaluation, margin analysis, and outcome prediction. Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated high diagnostic performance across multiple malignancies including breast, colorectal, prostate, lung, and gastrointestinal cancers. Emerging computational pathology platforms can predict molecular alterations directly from routine haematoxylin and eosin-stained slides, facilitating personalized treatment strategies while reducing dependence on expensive ancillary testing. AI-assisted pathology has also improved workflow efficiency, reduced interobserver variability, and enhanced diagnostic reproducibility. Importantly, AI-derived pathological insights are increasingly influencing surgical decision-making through improved risk stratification, optimized extent of resection, tailored lymphadenectomy, and prediction of treatment response.

items.title: Artificial intelligence at work: Balancing opportunity and fear in shaping employee well-being in the IT sector
items.abstract: BackgroundThis study investigates the complex relationship between perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) opportunities and well-being, exploring the underlying psychological processes. Using conservation of resources theory, we examine how employees who view AI as an opportunity report better workplace well-being and show greater adaptive thinking capacity. Conversely, perceptions of unemployment risk appear to be linked to challenges in cognitive reappraisal, which, in turn, correlate with diminished well-being.ObjectiveTo assess the relationships among these constructs, including the specific relationship between employment insecurity and well-being, to understand how AI is experienced as both a valuable tool and a source of stress.MethodsThis research, conducted among 201 professionals in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, uses convenience sampling and structural equation modeling (analyzed using SPSS and SmartPLS) to assess relationships among these constructs, including the relationship between employment insecurity and well-being.ResultsThe findings suggest that optimism and hope about AI may support psychological resilience, whereas concerns about displacement are negatively correlated with employee well-being.ConclusionUltimately, while grounded in a specific context, this study offers wider implications, showing how AI is experienced as both a valuable tool and a source of stress, depending largely on an individual's assessment of the related risks in their professional environment.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for full-cycle clinical management in orthokeratology: a comprehensive review
items.abstract: The global myopia epidemic, especially among children, poses a major public health burden. Orthokeratology (OK) is an established intervention for slowing myopia progression, yet its conventional practice is constrained by variable treatment responses, an experience-dependent fitting process, and the need for vigilant long-term safety monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers an approach to enhance precision, efficiency, and accessibility across the entire OK care cycle. This review assesses AI applications in OK, encompassing pre-treatment efficacy prediction, AI-assisted lens fitting and automated fit assessment during treatment, and post-treatment safety monitoring with complication risk alert. Evidence indicates that AI models perform comparably to, and in some tasks surpass, human experts in predicting outcomes and determining optimal lens parameters. However, translation from research to routine practice is hindered by limited data quality and diversity, the opacity of complex algorithms, insufficient external validation, and unresolved ethical concerns. Progress depends on building large-scale, diverse datasets, developing interpretable and robust models, and fostering effective human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Imbalanced Financial Classification and Its Societal Implications for Digital Trust: A Cost-Sensitive XGBoost–Transformer Ensemble
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates how financial institutions decide who is trusted, who is scrutinised, and who is refused — decisions that carry direct social consequences for individuals and communities. Automated credit-risk and fraud-assessment systems are deployed at a scale where their errors are not merely statistical but socially consequential, because they can restrict access to credit, widen financial exclusion, and erode public confidence in digital finance. This paper addresses one technical precondition for trustworthy deployment: reliable learning from severely imbalanced financial data. It treats the task as what the data actually measure — prediction of credit-card default rather than verified fraud — and proposes FraudShield, a hybrid framework that combines a gradient-boosting model (XGBoost), a Transformer-based tabular model, an adaptive gating mechanism that learns a per-instance weighting of the two branches, and a cost-sensitive decision layer that reflects the unequal social and economic cost of different errors. The framework is evaluated on the UCI Credit Card Default dataset (30,000 clients), whose positive (default) class comprises 22.12% of the observations — a ratio of approximately 1:3.52. The evaluation protocol splits the data before any preprocessing, fits target encoding and standardization within each training fold only, and applies SMOTE to the training folds alone. Under this corrected protocol, FraudShield attains an AUC-ROC of 0.943 and an F1-score of 0.892, and the cost-sensitive layer raises measured cost savings from 16.7% to 28.4% over the majority-class baseline. The paper interprets these results within a broader discussion of AI accountability, fairness, and digital trust, and argues that technically sound imbalanced-learning methods are a necessary — though not sufficient — condition for socially responsible automated decision-making in finance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Scientific Work: Ethics, Responsibility, and Practical Applications
items.abstract: Workshop held at the Leipzig University Library (more info here). Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific research, but how can we use these technologies responsibly? This workshop goes beyond simply presenting AI tools and instead focuses on the ethical, legal, and sustainable aspects of their application. We critically discuss how AI systems can influence scientific integrity, from data quality to potential biases in research results. Central to this are good scientific practice, data protection, copyright, and sustainability: How can researchers trustfully integrate AI tools without compromising reproducibility or ethical standards? We also explore ethical challenges such as transparency, fairness, and the long-term consequences of AI usage. Only after clarifying these core questions we address practical use: Which AI tools are suitable for which research goals? The workshop provides an insight into the opportunities and risks of AI in science, with the goal of equipping participants with a clear understanding of essential safeguards and best practices, as well as a practical, secure workflow to confidently integrate AI tools into their research without compromising scientific integrity, reproducibility, or compliance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in suicide prevention: promise, peril, and clinical implications for clinical practice
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry is progressing rapidly, with promising yet underexplored applications in suicide prevention. While most existing studies have focused on suicide risk prediction, AI could be applied more broadly across the suicide prevention continuum. This review explores AI's potential in improving the detection of suicidal ideation (SI), enhancing clinician training, and expanding patient access to psychotherapeutic support. Studies suggest that AI models may identify SI more sensitively than clinicians by detecting subtle linguistic or semantic cues. Furthermore, AI-based virtual patients have been shown to improve clinicians' confidence and accuracy in suicide risk assessments, particularly when used alongside traditional training methods. On the patient side, CBT-inspired AI tools offer scalable, on-demand support, but most remain unregulated and clinically unvalidated. Despite their perceived empathy and availability, such tools pose ethical and clinical risks. Many patients use AI tools without professional guidance, a trend clinicians often underestimate. This disconnect calls for urgent regulatory oversight and professional engagement. Without clear clinical validation, AI-based tools may evolve outside medical frameworks, exposing vulnerable individuals to preventable harm. Psychiatry must not only adapt but also lead, ensuring that innovation is harnessed responsibly to serve patients with empathy, safety, and scientific rigor.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Surrogacy: Legal Challenges, Liability, and the Protection of Vulnerable Parties
items.abstract: Despite the promise of better outcomes and efficiency, artificial intelligence in reproductive technology is changing the legal environment for surrogacy and complicating the family law landscape. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to match intended parents with surrogate mothers, conduct medical screenings and assist parents in making decisions. While the development is bringing benefits, the uncertainty created is uncontrolled. This paper examines the legal implications of AI-assisted surrogacy, focusing on issues of liability, contractual validity, and the determination of parental rights. The involvement of algorithmic systems challenges traditional legal principles, particularly in situations where harm may result from automated decisions or inaccurate data. The lack of transparency further complicates the allocation of responsibility among the different actors involved. From a human rights perspective, the use of AI in surrogacy raises concerns regarding the protection of the best interests of the child, as well as the autonomy and dignity of surrogate mothers. The paper highlights the risks of exploitation and unequal power relations, which may be intensified through technological mediation, especially in cross-border contexts. The paper argues that current legal frameworks are not adequately equipped to regulate the intersection between artificial intelligence and surrogacy, emphasizing the need for clearer legal standards and stronger regulatory oversight to ensure the protection of vulnerable parties.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness, Whistleblowing Systems, and Professional Skepticism in Higher-Education Fraud Detection
items.abstract: Background: Digital transformation has increased the complexity of fraud risks in higher education institutions, requiring governance mechanisms, professional judgment, and technological capabilities to operate in combination. Objective: This research investigates the influence of Whistleblowing Systems and Professional Skepticism on Fraud Detection Effectiveness while examining the direct and moderating roles of Artificial Intelligence Readiness. Methods: A quantitative methodology was employed through a cross-sectional survey involving internal auditors, members of Internal Supervisory Units (Satuan Pengawasan Internal [SPI]), and university staff engaged in governance and fraud prevention across Indonesian higher education institutions. The collected data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: The findings reveal that Whistleblowing Systems, Professional Skepticism, and Artificial Intelligence Readinesseach have a positive and statistically significant effect on Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Artificial Intelligence Readinessalso significantly strengthens the relationship between Whistleblowing Systems and Fraud Detection Effectiveness but does not significantly moderate the relationship between Professional Skepticism and Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Conclusion: These results suggest that artificial intelligence supports fraud detection not by replacing auditors' professional judgment but by strengthening organizational preparedness to integrate intelligent technologies into governance frameworks. Therefore, effective fraud detection in higher education depends on the synergy among organizational governance, human expertise, and Artificial Intelligence Readiness.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-based analysis of digital media engagement and user sentiment using machine learning techniques
items.abstract: Abstract Digital media datasets consist of both text content and platform, campaign, temporal, and engagement data, but precomputed sentiment and engagement data can lead to target leakage and overestimation of model performance. This study introduces the Hybrid Textual Sentiment Engagement Learning Model (HTSELM), a leakage-controlled late-fusion model for sentiment and engagement analysis. The experiments are conducted with the machine-generated Social Media Engagement Dataset, which has 28 raw columns and 12,000 records. Deterministic Affective Proxies are removed prior to training for the primary sentiment task. The text branch is a TF-IDF Linear Support Vector Machine with a weight of 0.70, and the structured branch is a HistGradientBoosting branch with a weight of 0.30, assigned by validation. On the held-out test set, HTSELM achieves an accuracy of 0.9392, macro-precision of 0.9471, macro-recall of 0.9336, macro-F1 of 0.9398, weighted-F1 of 0.9392, Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.9043, Cohen’s kappa of 0.9040, macro ROC-AUC of 0.9923, and macro PR-AUC of 0.9862. The Mean macro-F1 score for Exact 5-fold cross-validation is 0.9398 with an SD of 0.0069. Ablation shows that the dominant signal is text, and the validation-tuned fusion branch offers a relatively small but stable improvement over the text-only branch. There is minimal degradation due to numeric noise, but missing features and text corruption result in gradual degradation. A prospective engagement experiment (excluding engagement-rate components and post-response variables) is similarly close to chance, and the released pre-response variables are not reliable predictors of engagement. The results highlight the importance of leakage auditing, clear feature fusion and careful interpretation when analyzing digital media.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Visual–Inertial Navigation for Autonomous Lunar Surface Mobility: Systems, Datasets, Methods, and Open Challenges
items.abstract: Reliable onboard state estimation plays an important role in autonomous lunar surface mobility, given the lack of conventional global navigation satellite system (GNSS) coverage and the challenges of variable illumination and terrain texture. This review synthesizes model-based, learning-based, and hybrid visual–inertial odometry (VIO) approaches and assesses their relevance to lunar surface operations. The reviewed studies suggest that learned components can improve feature extraction, matching, depth estimation, and measurement confidence in selected datasets and operating conditions. However, representative lunar validation and uncertainty calibration remain limited. Given these limitations, hybrid architectures integrating learned components with explicit model-based estimators offer a comparatively testable design direction. Reduced lunar gravity alone does not render monocular scale unobservable; practical scale–bias performance also depends jointly on motion excitation, inertial quality, visual geometry, calibration, and estimation-window length. Stereo, wheel, crater, and map cues can provide additional metric information but introduce source-specific risks involving calibration, slip, association, and registration. Within the resources surveyed, we found no publicly available flight-derived lunar traverse dataset combining synchronized camera–IMU measurements, independent trajectory ground truth, and onboard timing. Evidence-based priorities include representative lunar validation, uncertainty-aware integration of learned components, consistency monitoring across metric sources, explicit estimator health and fallback mechanisms, and target-hardware resource evaluation.

items.title: Artificial Superintelligence: Must It Be Everywhere? From the Myth of Talos to Infrastructure Dependencies, Operational Authority, and Human Control
items.abstract: Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) raises important questions about the future of artificial intelligence, its potential benefits, and the possibility of losing human control. While many discussions focus on how powerful ASI could become, less attention is given to where it should be used, what authority it should have, and how its dependence on physical infrastructure may create additional risks. Using Talos, the bronze guardian of Greek mythology, as a metaphor for power and physical dependency, this article examines the differences between Artificial Intelligence (AI), Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and ASI. The study discusses their capabilities, shared infrastructure requirements, and the motivations behind the development of superintelligence. It also distinguishes risks already observed in current AI research from hypothetical scenarios involving future ASI systems. Specific attention is given to energy and critical infrastructure. The article explores the risks that may arise when an intelligent system is granted control over the infrastructure on which its own operation depends. It emphasizes that intelligence, autonomy, and operational authority are different concepts, and that greater intelligence does not necessarily require greater authority. The article proposes a selective, risk-based approach to ASI deployment, supported by limited access permissions, independent safety mechanisms, infrastructure resilience, and meaningful human oversight. Rather than assuming that superintelligence should be integrated into every system, it argues that its use should be determined by actual needs, expected benefits, resource requirements, and the ability to maintain effective human control.

items.title: Asesmen Pembelajaran SD Melalui Artificial Intelligence Berbantuan Zep Quiz Berbasis Adventure Game-Based Learning
items.abstract: Teachers’ limited capacity to develop engaging and adaptive digital assessments, coupled with the underutilization of artificial intelligence (AI), provided the basis for this community service program. The program aimed to improve teachers’ understanding and digital literacy in developing AI-assisted learning assessments using Zep Quiz within an adventure game-based learning approach. It was implemented at SDN 5 Mojolangu with teachers from the elementary school and Islamic elementary school teachers’ working group (KKG) in Lowokwaru District. The program comprised five stages: socialization, training, technology implementation, mentoring and evaluation, and sustainability planning. Its outcomes were evaluated using attendance records, questionnaires measuring understanding, perceived improvement in digital literacy, and program meaningfulness, as well as the products submitted by participants. The program involved 20 teachers, exceeding the initial target of 15 participants. The evaluation results showed a mean understanding score of 3.85 on a four-point scale, categorized as very high; a mean perceived digital literacy improvement score of 3.80, categorized as a substantial improvement; and a mean program meaningfulness score of 4.00, categorized as highly meaningful. All participants successfully developed and submitted 20 Zep Quiz products. These findings indicate that practice-oriented training and mentoring can help teachers integrate pedagogical considerations with technological skills in assessment development. Program sustainability will be supported through classroom trials, peer reviews within the KKG forum, and periodic evaluations to promote the independent and continuous use of digital assessment.

items.title: Assessing AI-Supported Problem-Solving in Young Adults Reporting Previous Learning-Disorder Diagnoses: Adaptation and Validation of the PS-AIRES and Preliminary Evaluation of a Claude-Based Training Program
items.abstract: AI-supported problem-solving environments increasingly require users to formulate effective prompts, iteratively refine interactions, critically evaluate outputs, and integrate AI assistance into coherent, self-directed solutions. Using a mixed-methods design, this two-phase study involved 672 participants across developmental, validation, and intervention stages. Study 1 included 12 participants in qualitative and cognitive interviewing, 40 independent participants in pilot testing, and 500 participants in the main validation sample. The study developed and psychometrically validated the Problem-Solving Skills in AI-Rich Environments Scale (PS-AIRES) and conducted a preliminary evaluation of a brief Claude-based training program. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a three-factor model comprising Strategic Task Framing and AI Instruction Design, Iterative Prompting and Response Refinement, and Verification, Critical Evaluation, and Integration. The model demonstrated satisfactory fit, high internal consistency, and acceptable temporal stability (ICC = 0.713, 95% CI [0.479, 0.852]). Measurement invariance across gender supported structural stability. A subsequent randomized pretest–posttest study involving an independent sample of 120 young adults reporting a previous specialist diagnosis of a learning disorder preliminarily evaluated the brief Claude-based training program. The findings provide initial evidence for the reliability and validity of PS-AIRES and suggest the short-term usefulness of structured, dyslexia-sensitive AI literacy training for enhancing problem-solving in AI-rich environments.

items.title: Augmenting colonoscopy with artificial intelligence and robotic assistance: a human-factors scoping review toward a task-based shared autonomy paradigm
items.abstract: Colonoscopy is central to colorectal cancer prevention but remains a high-demand psychomotor and cognitive procedure, characterized by operator dependency, variable performance, and substantial physical and mental workload. Increasing evidence links procedural quality and safety to clinician-related factors, including musculoskeletal strain, fatigue, and non-technical skills. Concurrently, artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic technologies are emerging as potential tools to address these limitations. We conducted a scoping review with narrative synthesis of literature on human factors, ergonomics, AI, robotic technologies, and shared autonomy in colonoscopy and surgical robotics. Evidence synthesis: Colonoscopy performance remains limited by non-negligible miss rates and variability driven by both technical and human factors. Ergonomic constraints and cognitive workload contribute significantly to operator strain and may affect vigilance and decision-making. AI systems-including computer-aided detection (CADe), diagnosis (CADx), and quality monitoring-have demonstrated improvements in detection metrics and procedural standardisation, although concerns regarding cognitive offloading and potential deskilling persist. In parallel, emerging robotic and soft-robotic platforms aim to enhance navigation, improve procedural ergonomics, and reduce operator musculoskeletal strain, although clinical evidence remains limited. These technologies converge within a task-based shared-autonomy paradigm integrating physical, perceptual, and cognitive augmentation, with different procedural tasks operating at different levels of human-system control. A task-based shared-autonomy framework may provide a coherent model for integrating AI and robotics into colonoscopy while preserving human supervision and clinical judgement. Future developments should prioritise human-centred design, workflow integration, and multidimensional evaluation strategies to ensure safe and effective clinical implementation.

items.title: Autonomous Robotic Systems in Agriculture 5.0: A Review on Technical Architecture, Operational Applications, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: This comprehensive narrative review examines the current state and future development perspectives of autonomous robotic systems within the scope of the Agriculture 5.0 paradigm, which aims for sustainable and efficient agricultural production. In this paper, the cognitive and physical structure of robotic systems is addressed through the "Eye-Brain-Foot Hand" hierarchy, and the role of next-generation Vision-Language Action (VLA) models, such as RT-2 and OpenVLA, in contextual agronomic decision-making processes is analyzed. Within the scope of field applications, the SAM2-based SPAF framework, which offers 95.54% harvesting success rate in tomatoes, and spot-spraying technologies that reduce chemical input volume by 90% are evaluated using quantitative data. Furthermore, the synergy between heterogeneous UAV-UGV fleets, trust-building through Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), and emerging advanced technological approaches such as Quantum Reinforcement Learning (QRL) are assessed. The results demonstrate that autonomous agriculture is not merely a tool to enhance technical efficiency, but is transforming into a cyber-physical production ecosystem where ethical responsibility, data sovereignty, and environmental sustainability converge.

items.title: Barriers and facilitators to healthcare artificial intelligence adoption in Wales: findings from focus groups
items.abstract: Background Building on a previous Wales-wide survey, this study aimed to provide more in-depth exploration of the barriers and facilitators to healthcare artificial intelligence adoption in Wales. Objectives The study aimed to explore these barriers and facilitators among various social groups, to inform policy development in Wales. Methods Four focus groups were conducted with a group of members of the public and a group of healthcare professionals (both groups recruited from a previous survey), as well as a group Sixth Form students and a group of retired adults. Inductive thematic analysis was used to generate themes and to compare the issues raised by the various groups. Contiguity-based analysis was undertaken to underscore how themes related with each other. Results A total of 21 individuals participated in the focus groups (healthcare professionals=6, members of the public=6, sixth-form students=5, retirees=4). Seven thematic networks were identified. Across groups, seven themes were identified in the healthcare professional group, six in the general members of the public group, seven in the sixth form student group, and seven in the retiree group. All groups voiced concerns about data privacy and highlighted the importance of human oversight of AI and human contact during the clinical encounter as they expressed more trust in human practitioners. There were though differences between groups, such as greater trust in black-box systems by healthcare professionals, and between individual participants in regard to trust in private organisations developing AI for healthcare organisations. Conclusions All groups were concerned with information security and expressed a preference for human contact during the clinical encounter and a human-in-the-loop approach. There were differences between the groups, such as in attitudes towards black-box AI technologies and trust in clinicians. No additional barriers or facilitators were identified for proxy consent.

items.title: Basic psychological need satisfaction profiles at work: person-centered links to job crafting and intrinsic motivation
items.abstract: Grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this study adopted a person-centered approach to investigate whether job crafting behaviors are associated with employees’ membership in basic psychological need satisfaction profiles. Previous research has focused on contextual workplace factors such as job demands-resources and managerial behaviors, with less attention given to employees’ proactive role in influencing their motivational experiences. This study addresses this gap by identifying basic psychological need satisfaction profiles among employees in South African small and medium enterprises. It further examines whether job crafting predicts profile membership and whether these profiles differ in intrinsic motivation. A cross-sectional survey with 197 employees was conducted. They completed the Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale–Work Domain, Job Crafting Questionnaire, and Multidimensional Work Motivation Scale. Latent profile analysis supported three quantitatively differentiated profiles reflecting low, moderate, and high need satisfaction. In classification-error-adjusted analyses, job crafting dimensions were associated with profile membership. Higher task and cognitive crafting differentiated the high from the moderate profile, whereas cognitive and relational crafting differentiated the moderate from the low profile. Sensitivity analyses indicated that estimates contrasting the high and low profiles were imprecise and should be interpreted cautiously. Intrinsic motivation differed significantly across the profiles, with employees in the high need satisfaction profile reporting the highest intrinsic motivation. These findings extend person-centered research on SDT by showing that proactive job crafting behaviors are associated with employees’ membership in more adaptive need satisfaction groups.

items.title: Behavioral differentiation during the AIGC image generation waiting period: effects on creativity in conceptual design
items.abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) offers new ways to generate inspiration for conceptual design, yet limited attention has been paid to the waiting period between prompt submission and AI image output. This study examined behavioral differentiation during this interval and investigated how the task relevance and cognitive load of waiting-period behaviors affect creativity in conceptual design. Methods Three experiments were conducted with design students. Experiment 1 identified and classified core waiting-period behaviors ( N = 30); Experiment 2 measured the cognitive load of representative behaviors using the NASA-TLX ( N = 24); and Experiment 3 employed a behavior-based 2 × 2 conceptual framework ( N = 60), in which four representative waiting-period behaviors were selected to represent different combinations of task relevance (high/low) and relative workload (higher/lower), and their creative performance was compared. Results The results showed that the AIGC generation waiting period was not a passive interval but involved multiple identifiable behavioral patterns. Creative performance differed across the four representative behavioral conditions. Specifically, the overall creativity score in the GP condition was significantly lower than the scores in the RS, DB, and RB conditions, whereas no significant differences were observed among the latter three conditions. These findings further suggest that the subsequent influence of waiting-period behaviors on creativity may depend not only on the level of cognitive demand but also on whether cognitive resources remain directed toward the ongoing creative task. Discussion This study further interprets AIGC generation waiting-period behaviors from three interrelated functional perspectives: task continuity, cognitive expenditure, and temporary disengagement/incubation. This functional account provides an empirical basis for understanding the cognitive role of the AIGC generation waiting period and for optimizing AI-assisted conceptual design workflows.

items.title: Behavioural Sociology of Humans and Machines
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly participates in communication, decision-making, and collective action, making the social organisation of human-machine interaction central to Hybrid Intelligence (HI). This chapter reviews the behavioural sociology of humans and machines through an HI lens, examining how interaction and feedback shape the combination of human and artificial capabilities. Drawing on sociology, social psychology, human-computer interaction, organisational studies, collective intelligence, and science and technology studies, it traces processes from individual social perception to cooperation in hybrid groups and organisational and institutional arrangements. Particular attention is given to how machine participation alters familiar mechanisms: social categorisation attaches expectations to designed identities, reciprocity may involve unequal social obligations, and algorithmic recommendations acquire authority through organisational practices. The chapter distinguishes observable machine behaviour from human interpretations of intention, understanding, and moral responsibility. It also considers how behavioural effects can extend beyond direct human-machine encounters, while separating established findings from proposed longer-term consequences. It argues that the benefits of HI depend on how roles, incentives, reliance, and accountability are organised, and identifies priorities for empirical research on these evolving sociotechnical arrangements.

items.title: Benefits and Drawbacks of Using Artificial Intelligence to Manage Human Resources in the Tourism Industry of Vulnerable Areas: A Case Study of Jammu and Kashmir
items.abstract: This present study examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping Human Resource Management (HRM) within the tourism sector of Jammu and Kashmir, a region that depends heavily on tourism yet faces persistent political and social instability. Drawing insights from 15 semi-structured interviews with HR managers, tourism operators, and employees, the research identifies three major themes: digital literacy, trust deficit, and AI-driven opportunities. While nearly 80% of respondents acknowledged AI&s;s potential to simplify recruitment and enhance training, most also expressed concerns about inconsistent internet access, limited awareness, and job insecurity. The findings suggest that AI, though promising, cannot be viewed as a quick solution. Its successful integration will depend on gradual adoption, transparent practices, and active collaboration among government bodies, HR professionals, and tourism authorities to build AI readiness in such sensitive regions.

items.title: BEYOND AUTOMATION: REFRAMING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN EDUCATION THROUGH COGNITIVE AUTONOMY, ADAPTIVE LEARNING, AND HUMAN–AI COLLABORATION
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is transforming instructional practices, assessment methods, and the relationship between teachers and learners. However, the educational value of AI cannot be determined solely by its ability to automate tasks or generate information. This paper examines AI-supported education through three interconnected dimensions: cognitive autonomy, adaptive learning pathways, and human–AI collaboration. Drawing on international research and educational policy frameworks, the study adopts a conceptual and analytical approach to identify opportunities, challenges, and principles for responsible AI integration. Particular attention is given to students' independent reasoning, critical evaluation of AI-generated content, personalized instruction, and teachers' professional judgement. The paper proposes a conceptual model, termed the Attempt–Assist–Evaluate–Transfer model, which encourages learners to attempt tasks independently, receive targeted AI support, evaluate generated information, and transfer their knowledge to unfamiliar situations without assistance. The analysis suggests that effective AI integration requires more than technological access; it requires pedagogical planning, ethical safeguards, and assessment strategies that prioritize genuine learning. The paper concludes that AI should function as a supportive educational resource rather than a substitute for human reasoning or professional teaching.

items.title: Beyond curricular inclusion: An indigenous knowledge sovereignty framework for South African technology teacher education in the AI era
items.abstract: Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) are increasingly visible in curriculum policy, yet visibility can coexist with weak community authority over how knowledge is selected, interpreted, digitised and assessed. This conceptual article develops and theoretically grounds RELATE as a community-accountable framework for evaluating and designing Indigenous knowledge engagement in South African Technology teacher education. A bounded critical integrative conceptual synthesis connected 21 substantive sources across four domains: IKS in science, STEM and Technology Education; epistemic justice and decoloniality; culturally sustaining and Indigenous methodologies; and Indigenous data and artificial-intelligence governance. Sources were purposively selected for conceptual relevance, South African specificity where available, traceability and evidentiary contribution; policy, legal, empirical and conceptual claims were coded separately. The synthesis identifies four recurring deficits: representation without epistemic parity; contextualisation without community authority; digitisation without governance; and innovation without ecological or distributive accountability. RELATE responds through six interdependent dimensions: Recognition, Ethical reciprocity, Local authority, Apprenticeship and agency, Technological translation, and Ecological responsibility. The framework treats these dimensions as a non-linear governance architecture rather than causal stages. It extends adjacent approaches by integrating curriculum, pedagogy, community decision rights, technological mediation and ecological accountability within one Technology-teacher-education framework. RELATE is a theoretically derived proposal, not a validated intervention or measurement instrument. Its contribution is to make authority, permission, benefit, restriction and contestation assessable features of programme design and future empirical inquiry.

items.title: Beyond Risk: Sexual Health Vulnerability in University Students
items.abstract: Aim: To examine multilevel sexual-health vulnerability in higher education and distinguish evidence about knowledge, preventive behaviour, service use and infection-related outcomes. Subject and Methods: The authors conducted a structured critical review of a pre-existing 118-reference bibliography, retaining a publication boundary of 25 May 2026. The reference-based evidence map was documented on 8 October 2026. Sources were classified by population, design and relevance; 38 candidate reports received content-level assessment. Source-linked information and the availability of supporting material were recorded. The review was human-led, with artificial intelligence used as an assistive tool. Results: Thirty-three empirical higher-education reports were charted and 85 references retained as context. The mapped reports comprised 18 cross-sectional analyses, six randomised trials, five other intervention evaluations, three qualitative studies and one participatory mixed-methods study. They described gaps between knowledge and practice, uneven testing and vaccine uptake, and barriers involving confidentiality, stigma and service design. Digital interventions had outcome-specific findings: educational gains did not consistently translate into behaviour or vaccination. Companion reports and mixed denominators precluded summing participants. The documentation supporting many charted fields was limited to abstracts or excerpts. Conclusion: University prevention should connect education and behavioural capability with accessible testing, biomedical prevention and continuity of care. The proposed five-level framework is a service-design and research proposition, not a validated risk score. The bounded bibliography and uneven source documentation limit completeness and certainty.

items.title: Beyond Seamlessness: Mobile AI and Situated Sense-Making
items.abstract: This commentary explores what it means for generative artificial intelligence (AI) to become mobile, as interaction shifts from screen-bound querying to AI participation in the flow of everyday situations. Rather than framing this shift in terms of access or use, it approaches mobile AI through situated sense-making, understood here in terms of the constitution of sense through ongoing activities, embodied cues, social coordination, and mobile communication affordances as AI becomes part of the situation. Starting from a café interaction staged in a promotional video for a future AI device, the commentary confronts corporate claims of seamless interaction with theoretical accounts of situated sense-making. Drawing on mobile communication studies and human–machine communication (HMC), it argues that mobile AI requires a specification of sense-making as HMC's central boundary object: not only as mutual interpretation between users and interfaces but also as a process embedded in ongoing activities and interactions. The commentary develops this argument through three interrelated aspects of situated sense-making—coordination, distribution, and stabilization—showing how mobile AI may reshape participation, redistribute epistemic authority, and steer relevance toward either shared problematization or premature closure. It thereby advances an approach to analyzing and designing embodied AI that foregrounds visible coordination, responsive alignment, and stabilization that remains open to collective deliberation.

items.title: Beyond Technocentrism in AI-Supported Special Education: The PAISEN Model of Teacher-Mediated Inclusive Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new possibilities for inclusive teaching and learning for students with special educational needs (SEN), yet AI-in-SEN research remains largely technocentric, often describing system capabilities without explaining how outputs become pedagogically meaningful. This conceptual paper develops the PAISEN Model (Pedagogical Artificial Intelligence for Special Education Needs) through an integrative synthesis of AI in education, inclusive pedagogy, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and assistive technology. The model proposes a non-deterministic sequence in which AI Teaching Support Systems provide data and adaptive affordances, Teacher Pedagogical Mediation interprets and contextualises them, and an Inclusive Learning Environment translates decisions into accessible participation opportunities. SEN learning outcomes are treated as proposed consequences rather than established effects. Teacher AI competency, institutional support, digital infrastructure, and learner characteristics function as boundary conditions, while an adaptive feedback loop links learner evidence to teacher reflection and instructional adjustment. The novelty of PAISEN lies in making teacher judgement the central explanatory mechanism and separating technology, pedagogical processes, learning conditions and moderators. Theoretically, it bridges AIED and inclusive education; pedagogically, it clarifies differentiated and UDL-aligned AI use without replacing teacher agency; practically, it provides a testable structure for implementation and evaluation. The proposed relationships require empirical validation in authentic SEN settings.

items.abstract: This article explores the pedagogical potential of using artificial intelligence tools to develop individual learning pathways for primary school pupils, taking into account their educational needs, cognitive abilities, and individual learning pace. Particular attention is given to adaptive learning, the personalization of learning tasks, the analysis of learning outcomes, and the timely provision of pedagogical support. The study emphasizes the importance of maintaining the teacher’s leading role in integrating artificial intelligence into primary education, considering children’s developmental and psychological characteristics, ensuring digital safety, and supporting independent thinking. It also examines how the purposeful and pedagogically grounded use of artificial intelligence can improve learning effectiveness, strengthen pupils’ motivation, and support the educational development of every child.

items.title: Bots, Trust, and Generative AI: Framing Communicative Agency in a Small-Language Media Context
items.abstract: This article examines how bots, chatbots, and generative AI are represented as forms of communicative agency in a small-language media environment. It draws on a mixed content analysis of 195 digital news items published by 1TV.ge, Euronews Georgia, Imedi News, and Rustavi 2 between September 15, 2024, and December 31, 2025, a fifteen-and-a-half-month period spanning parts of two calendar years. Rather than evaluating AI systems technically or measuring audience responses, the article analyzes how news coverage assigns roles to automated and AI-based systems through publication patterns, outlet profiles, dominant frames, functional emphases, trust narratives, risk discourse, media literacy elements, and named AI systems. The corpus was most often organized through a technological or business news frame (93 items; 47.7%). Other frames included myth-nightmare (36; 18.5%), media literacy/fact-checking (26; 13.3%), global political competition/information war (24; 12.3%), and myth-idyll (16; 8.2%). The comparison shows that Euronews Georgia emphasized international and security-related coverage, Imedi News foregrounded education and textual interaction, Rustavi 2 emphasized consumer-facing products and visual applications, and 1TV.ge displayed a comparatively balanced explanatory profile. The article argues that bot transformation is better understood as a change in communicative roles than as a simple replacement of older automation by AI chatbots. In this process, agency, usefulness, trust, risk, and responsibility intersect. The Georgian-language case contributes to Human-Machine Communication, AI-mediated communication, and media-framing research by showing how global AI debates are localized outside dominant English-language media environments. Coding was conducted by a single researcher; an intracoder stability check on 20 items (approximately 10% of the corpus) produced no changes to dominant-frame assignments.

items.title: Bridging communication gaps across the biomedical ecosystem
items.abstract: The current landscape of science communication is undergoing rapid transformation, shaped by profound societal shifts including the COVID-19 pandemic, the rise of social media, the decline of traditional news media, and the growing influence of large language models. These changes have fundamentally altered how the biomedical community and the public share, consume, and trust scientific information. This article contextualizes these changes, explains why redesigning the science communication ecosystem is urgent, and offers recommendations to improve accuracy, strengthen trust, and deepen public engagement. Specifically, philanthropy can play a key role by driving momentum and optimizing the flow of scientific information across three stages: (1) scientific discovery to publication, (2) interpretation and distribution, and (3) public engagement.

items.title: Bridging the digital divide in online political participation. Six inclusion infrastructuring strategies
items.abstract: Digital democracy platforms are promoted as scalable tools to broaden citizen participation, yet they commonly attract limited and socially patterned engagement. This article asks how participation promoters attempt to reduce digital inequalities in platform-based political processes and make “inclusive participation” practically possible. It draws on an international qualitative dataset combining 65 semi-structured interviews conducted between 2019 and 2026 with platform developers, public servants, civic tech activists, consultants, and NGO leaders, complemented by platform and document analysis, press material, and ethnographic observations of participatory assemblies and events. The analysis identifies six inclusion infrastructuring strategies, ordered from mediatized to more human-based interventions: technical solutions, communication, fixed supports, social events, mobile supports, and face-to-face settings. Across cases, inclusion emerges as ongoing organizational work that extends platforms through staff, physical devices, partnerships, and coordinated outreach. Overall, the article shows how inclusion is actively infrastructured through heterogeneous sociotechnical arrangements, while their effects on participatory inequalities remain context-dependent and insufficiently evaluated.

items.title: Bridging theory and tender practice in ESG contractor selection: a social network analysis of public sector construction procurement
items.abstract: Public procurement is increasingly used to pursue environmental, social and governance (ESG) objectives in construction, yet the ESG criteria emphasised in procurement practice do not always align with those advanced in the academic literature. This study examines that gap through a comparative social network analysis (SNA) of two datasets: 46 New Zealand public sector construction tender documents and 39 peer reviewed studies. Co-occurrence networks were constructed for practice and theory, and degree centrality (DC) was used to identify structurally prominent ESG criteria. The findings show clear divergence between the two domains. Procurement practice gave greater prominence to workforce development, training, inclusion, and workforce well-being, whereas the literature placed stronger emphasis on occupational health and safety, energy efficiency, material reuse and recycling, waste management, and greenhouse gas reduction. These differences indicate a tenderability gap, in which criteria become central in procurement not only because they are conceptually important, but also because they can be specified, evidenced at tender stage, and monitored contractually. Tenderability therefore explains why ESG priorities are selectively amplified or muted as they move from theory into tender evaluation. The study consolidates the results into a validated, practice-oriented ESG criteria framework organised around tender evaluation logic, providing a more grounded basis for embedding ESG and circular economy objectives into public sector construction procurement.

items.abstract: Documents containing binding legal terms and risk obligations remain largely unread, particularly in multilingual contexts where regulatory systems vary across jurisdictions. This paper presents a multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to identify potentially risky clauses across Arabic, English and French legal, regulatory and contractual documents, instantiated on Algerian legislation as a fully specified reference framework. In addition, we introduce a visual analytics system tailored for legal domain experts, integrating the underlying datasets, model outputs and evaluation results to support interactive analysis and model interpretability. The system’s knowledge base is grounded in a trilingual corpus of 2535 sentences, comprising 315 fully annotated clauses whose cross-lingual legal equivalence was verified by a panel of ten legal experts. Performance evaluation was conducted on EVAL-EEM, an external corpus of 81 annotated passages extracted from 55 real-world sources. Because EVAL-EEM was used during development for decision-configuration tuning, it is characterised as a development corpus rather than a strictly held-out test set; consequently, both in-sample metrics and nested cross-validated estimates are reported. On the binary risk-identification task, the proposed system improves from an initial F1 score of 0.340 to 0.806 in the final in-sample evaluation and 0.792 under nested cross-validation. GPT-4o without retrieval achieves an F1 score of 0.775, showing no statistically significant difference from the complete RAG architecture (p=0.39), whereas supervised baselines, including a fine-tuned XLM-R, exhibit substantially lower performance on external documents. These empirical findings demonstrate the potential of statute-grounded multilingual LLM reasoning augmented by traceable retrieval evidence. However, because configuration selection was conducted on the evaluation corpus itself, these results should be interpreted as preliminary and specific to the evaluated knowledge base, dataset and legal visual analytics system. Further validation on larger, unexposed benchmarks, along with formal user studies, is necessary to establish cross-jurisdictional portability, empirical generalizability and system usability.

items.title: C2 multi-agent factory: large-small model collaboration empowering a new command and control paradigm
items.abstract: Abstract Command and control (C2) is an agile crisis management architecture for highly uncertain emergencies, originating from military operations but now widely deployed in public safety emergency response, traffic and airspace management, industrial energy systems, urban governance, and large-scale event coordination. Traditional C2 systems mainly rely on preset rules, static processes and manual decision-making, which expose obvious limitations in the face of modern environments with high dynamics, complex disturbances and incomplete information. Aiming at the significant problems of traditional command and control systems, such as structural rigidity, information overload, decision lag, and insufficient collaboration, based on the concepts of software factory and single-agent factory, combined with the latest progress of large-small model collaboration in the field of command and control, this paper proposes a new paradigm of large-small model collaboration empowering command and control—the concept of C2 multi-agent factory, which upgrades the single-agent factory that produces “individual intelligence” to a multi-agent factory that produces and runs “swarm intelligence”, and is combined with the command and control system and its application scenarios. The overall system architecture of the C2 multi-agent factory and the large-small model collaboration mechanism based on the C2 multi-agent factory are given. Finally, an application example is given to further illustrate how the C2 multi-agent factory can use the large-small model collaboration technology to empower command and control. The C2 multi-agent factory proposed in this paper will find a new path for the construction of an evolvable intelligent command and control system, promote the substantive leap of artificial intelligence towards the C2 system.

items.title: Calibrating LLM Explanations to Human Decisions with Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Explanations of LLM outputs are considered an important way to make model behavior legible, helping human users make good decisions on downstream tasks. However, default training approaches for improving explanations target model task performance or human preference rather than human decision quality. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{HD-RL}, a reinforcement learning framework for optimizing LLM explanations for human decision making. Our approach calibrates a human decision simulator on observed human decisions, applying a proxy reward model to optimize the LLM to generate explanations that help people to make good decisions. We apply this framework to AI-generated text detection. In our initial data collection phase, we observed that while LLMs possess strong autonomous detection capabilities, the explanations they generate for users yield near-random human accuracy (51.3\%). By applying the HD-RL framework to the open-source Qwen 3.6 model, we generate optimized explanations that improve human performance, achieving a GLMM-estimated human accuracy of 63.7\% in a randomized between-subjects experiment with repeated measures and outperforming RLVR, RLAIF, and other baselines by over 8\%.

items.title: Camera-Based AI-Assisted Scoring for the Balance Error Scoring System: A Cross-sectional Validity and Agreement Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Balance Error Scoring System (BESS) is widely used to assess static postural control in sports medicine and rehabilitation. However, conventional real-time scoring is observer dependent and may be influenced by rater experience, viewing angle, attention, and the interpretation of transient or overlapping errors. This study evaluated the criterion-related validity and agreement of a camera-based artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted BESS relative to consensus video-review manual scoring and compared its error magnitude with on-site manual scoring. METHODS: This single-center cross-sectional study included 80 of 84 recruited participants: 40 healthy controls, 20 with chronic ankle instability (CAI), and 20 after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). All participants completed the standard six-condition BESS protocol. Scores were obtained using AI-assisted, on-site manual, and consensus video-review manual scoring; the latter was prespecified as the pragmatic manual reference standard. Primary total-score analyses included Pearson correlation, the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), Bland-Altman mean difference and 95% limits of agreement (LoA), mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean square error (RMSE). Condition- and group-specific analyses were exploratory. RESULTS: For the total BESS score, AI-assisted scoring versus the reference showed r = 0.989, ICC = 0.989 (95% CI 0.982-0.993), a mean difference of 0.188 errors, 95% LoA from -2.063 to 2.438 errors, an MAE of 0.787 errors, and an RMSE of 1.157 errors. On-site manual scoring versus the reference showed r = 0.922, ICC = 0.920 (95% CI 0.877-0.948), a mean difference of -0.612 errors, 95% LoA from -6.680 to 5.455 errors, an MAE of 2.212 errors, and an RMSE of 3.136 errors. Condition-specific discrepancies were larger in the single-leg and tandem-stance conditions. Exploratory group comparisons showed higher total BESS scores in individuals with CAI than in healthy controls. CONCLUSIONS: Camera-based AI-assisted BESS scoring showed strong total-score agreement with the pragmatic manual reference standard and smaller discrepancies than on-site manual scoring. This approach may support more standardized BESS assessment; however, external validation and longitudinal reliability testing are required before interchangeability with manual scoring can be considered.

items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Personalize Learning? An Analysis of AI-Based Adaptive Learning Systems for Senior School Students
items.abstract: Most classrooms still move at one speed. A teacher with thirty or forty students has to choose a pace that suits the middle of the class, which leaves weaker students behind and keeps stronger students waiting. AI-based adaptive learning systems promise to change this by watching how each student answers, estimating what that student already knows, and choosing the next task to match. This paper examines how far that promise holds for senior school students. It explains how adaptive systems work in simple terms, reviews findings from major meta-analyses and field experiments, including a randomised study of the Mindspark program in Delhi, and compares adaptive learning with the traditional one-size-fits-all approach. The evidence suggests that well-designed adaptive systems produce real and sometimes large learning gains, with reported effect sizes between about 0.2 and 0.8 standard deviations, and that students who are furthest behind often gain the most. However, the gains depend heavily on how the system is designed and how it is used. Systems that simply give answers can weaken learning, and results shrink when teachers are not involved. The paper concludes that AI can personalise practice, feedback and pacing to a significant extent, but it cannot replace the motivational, social and judgement-based work of a teacher. A blended model, in which AI handles adaptive practice and teachers use the data to guide instruction, is proposed for Indian senior schools.

items.title: Cardiometabolic Assessment in Patients with Overweight, Obesity, or Type 2 Diabetes Undergoing Artificial Intelligence–Based Retinal Screening: A Real-World Evidence Study
items.abstract: Background: Overweight, obesity, and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) increase the risk of vascular complications, including retinal vascular alterations. Artificial intelligence (AI)—based retinal screening enables early detection of microvascular damage, potentially contributing to appropriate cardiometabolic prevention strategies. We performed a realworld evidence observational study to assess cardiometabolic parameters as well as retinal vascular alterations using novel AI-based retinal imaging. Methods: Between September and December 2025, we recruited 301 consecutive adults with overweight,obesity, or T2DM; cardiometabolic assessment was performed, and all participants also underwent retinal screening with the Aireen AI system, distinguishing those who resulted positive ( n = 42), negative ( n = 204), or undetermined ( n = 55) at the screening. Results: All patients who resulted positive at the screening were confirmed with a diagnosis of retinal alterations by the ophthalmologists. The presence of positive retinal screening (RS+) progressively increased with worsening fasting glycemia, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels, carotid intima–media thickness, and endothelial function ( P < 0.001 for all). Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed independent associations of RS+ with HbA1c [odds ratio (OR) 2.29, P < 0.001], carotid stenosis (OR 1.06, P < 0.001), fasting glucose (OR 1.02, P < 0.001), and the triglyceride/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (OR 2.19, P = 0.010). Conclusions: These findings suggest that AIbased retinal screening with advanced tools can effectively identify early microvascular damage in individuals with overweight, obesity, or T2DM, with RS+ prevalence reflecting glycemic burden and vascular dysfunction. Therefore, integrating AI retinal assessment into cardiometabolic prevention programs may enable timely interventions to prevent progression to vision-threatening complications and support comprehensive cardiovascular risk management.

items.title: Cervical Cancer Burden in Africa: An Integrative Review of Epidemiology, Plant Medicine, and AI-Driven Innovation
items.abstract: Cervical cancer imposes a heavy burden in low- and middle-income countries and persistently high incidence and mortality in Sub-Saharan Africa due to unequal access to prevention and care. Although human papillomavirus (HPV) is a major driving factor, the risk is amplified by HIV co-infection, socioeconomic barriers, limited infrastructure, low health literacy, and behavioral factors, leading to frequent late-stage diagnosis, low screening coverage, and poor survival. Recent expansion of HPV vaccination programs since 2019 has achieved high coverage in some countries, but continent-wide rates remain below targets amid hesitancy, inequities, and systemic weaknesses. Thus, there is a critical need for an integrated synthesis of multidisciplinary evidence that reflects the peculiarities and diversities of African health systems. Moreover, high mortality rates underscore the need for integrated, context-specific evidence to strengthen vaccination, screening, and management strategies in line with WHO global elimination targets. Plant medicine promises to complement mainstream health delivery in low resource settings. Emerging artificial intelligence (AI) tools show strong potential to improve screening accuracy, reduce subjectivity and resource needs, and enhance early detection in resource-limited settings. This review synthesizes multidisciplinary data on economic impact, epidemiology, risk factors, prevention, diagnostic challenges, plant medicine and AI innovations to guide equitable progress in diverse African contexts.

items.title: Charting the rise of artificial intelligence in medical education: a global bibliometric and network analysis, 2000–2026
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence has moved from a peripheral curiosity to a core feature of modern medical education through adaptive learning, simulation-based training, automated assessment, and large language models such as ChatGPT. Publication activity has accelerated rapidly, but the structure of this expanding literature has not been comprehensively mapped. METHODS: Bibliographic data were obtained from the Web of Science Core Collection using a search strategy that combined medical education terms in the title field with artificial intelligence terms in the topic field. Articles, review articles, and data papers published from 2000 to 2026 were included. A total of 2,298 records were retrieved. Microsoft Excel was used for descriptive analyses, and VOSviewer (version 1.6.20) was used to construct keyword co-occurrence, country collaboration, and institutional collaboration networks. Data for 2026 represent a partial calendar year. RESULTS: Publication output remained limited until the late 2010s and rose sharply after 2021. Of the 2,298 records, 2,066 (89.9%) were published from 2021 to 2026, with the highest complete-year output in 2025 (821 publications). The United States led in publication volume (918 records) and raw citation count (14,582 citations), followed by the People's Republic of China (367 records; 4,404 citations). The Journal of Surgical Education published the most articles. Harvard Medical School led institutional output, whereas Stanford University and the University of California San Francisco had higher raw citation totals despite fewer publications. Artificial intelligence, medical education, ChatGPT, medical students, and machine learning were the most prominent keywords. CONCLUSIONS: Artificial intelligence in medical education is a rapidly expanding but geographically and institutionally concentrated field. Raw citation patterns differed from publication volume, although these unadjusted measures should not be interpreted as direct comparisons of research quality. Thematic patterns emphasize learner-facing applications, assessment, and generative AI, while responsible curricular integration and empirical evaluation remain important priorities. These findings are especially relevant to emergency medicine education, where simulation, time-sensitive decision-making, and competency assessment are central.

items.title: ChatGPT adoption and responsible use in Vietnamese transnational education students’ academic writing
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how cognitive and affective factors drive Vietnamese transnational education (TNE) students' intention to use ChatGPT for English academic writing, and investigates how information verification and responsible use enhance English writing proficiency (EWP). Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 501 TNE students across three major Vietnamese cities were analysed using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The conceptual model integrates the technology acceptance model, the pupils’ attitudes toward technology short questionnaire (PATT-SQ) model and Mitcham’s philosophical framework. Insights from an expert survey of six lecturers supported the interpretation and practical implications. Findings Cognitive factors (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use and perceived risk) significantly influence ChatGPT usage intention, whereas affective factors do not. Perceived risk negatively impacts intention, reflecting student awareness of potential drawbacks. The results further reveal a strong behavioural pathway in which frequent use intention promotes information verification, which fosters responsible use and ultimately improves EWP. This demonstrates that learning outcomes depend on critical, ethical engagement rather than usage frequency alone. Research limitations/implications Higher education institutions (HEI) should embed AI literacy, verification practices and ethical guidelines into curricula to optimise ChatGPT utility and mitigate dependency. Limitations include a cross-sectional design, lack of contextual factors and a localised sample, which future longitudinal and comparative studies should address. Originality/value This study offers one of the first empirical examinations linking ChatGPT adoption, verification behaviours, responsible use and measurable EWP gains among Vietnamese TNE students. By integrating cognitive, affective, behavioural and ethical dimensions, it extends traditional technology adoption models to the context of generative AI-assisted academic writing.

items.title: Cloud-Based Infrastructure for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Workloads: A Scalable Framework for Saudi Enterprises
items.abstract: In Saudi companies artificial intelligence and machine learning are moving from being mere experiments to becoming operational capabilities, which is leading to an infrastructure issue that goes well beyond the need for computing power. The processes involved in training, fine-tuning, inference, feature preparation, model monitoring, governance and retraining all have diverse requirements for accelerators, storage, networking, data locality, elasticity and reliability. This review draws on research carried out between 2020 and 2025 in order to look at how cloud architecture can support these types of workloads on an enterprise level while taking into account the Saudi situation regarding rapid digital transformation, the adoption of cloud services, data governance and the modernisation of various sectors. The review applies a structured evidence-synthesis approach focused on infrastructure architecture, workload orchestration, MLOps, cloud-edge distribution, security, reliability, cost control and organisational readiness. The evidence shows that scalable AI infrastructure should be viewed as a coordinated platform rather than as a set of separate services; effective designs incorporate elastic pools of CPU and GPU resources, container orchestration, tiered data services, automated model pipelines, observability, policy controls, workload-aware scheduling and selective edge execution. The Saudi Enterprise AI Cloud Framework proposed in this review combines these capabilities into six layers and includes a closed operational loop that links demand prediction, placement, execution, telemetry, policy evaluation and lifecycle learning. The review maintains that scalability must be assessed together with availability, cost predictability, data sovereignty, operational resilience and discipline in managing the model lifecycle. It ends with an implementation roadmap and a research agenda for businesses that wish to industrialise AI as part of their digital transformation aligned with Vision 2030.

items.title: Cognitive Authorities in Science Education Classroom: A Nexus Analysis on Inquiry-Based Tasks
items.abstract: This qualitative study examined how cognitive authority is distributed, negotiated, and constructed during science learning tasks at Mindoro State University–Calapan City Campus, Philippines. Using nexus analysis, the study investigated an analytical chemistry class involving one teacher and 13 second-year Bachelor of Secondary Education students. Data were collected through observations and audiovisual recordings of two classroom sessions—lecture-discussion and hands-on experiments—and semi-structured interviews with the teacher and five students. Transcribed data were coded using NVivo 15, with analysis focusing on social actions, classroom interaction, and the use of potentially authoritative information sources. Findings revealed that cognitive authority varied with task structure. During lecture-discussion, authority centered on the teacher’s expertise and instructional materials, while hands-on experiments provided opportunities for students to negotiate interpretations through peer exchanges, procedural questioning, and experimental observations. Students drew on teacher-provided resources, prior knowledge, personal experiences, and laboratory evidence, and reported consulting academic journals, websites, and generative artificial intelligence. Interview accounts indicated attempts to corroborate digital information, although verification during work completed outside the classroom was not directly observed. The findings suggest that cognitive authority is relational and shaped by interactions among participants, learning resources, and task demands. The study highlights the importance of designing science activities that combine teacher guidance with opportunities for collaborative reasoning and explicit evaluation of evidence and source credibility. These context-specific insights can inform instructional design and teacher development aimed at supporting student agency and responsible knowledge construction.
